<reason>Both sides argued competently, but CON built the more decisive logical trap and closed it out. CON's key move was showing that PRO's concrete replacement standard — a presumption of discharge after a time-and-income threshold, rebuttable only if the lender proves "realistic near-term ability to pay" — cannot coexist with PRO's own deterrence claim that filing pain alone stops gaming. If filing-cost deters strategic borrowing, the substantive standard needn't change at all (which is CON's position); if the standard must change to a lender-unrebuttable presumption, then the claimed deterrent evaporates, since lenders have no visibility into future earnings and can essentially never rebut it. PRO never squarely answers this epistemic-asymmetry problem in Rebuttal 2 or Closing, instead reasserting that "judges still decide" and that "any sharpening that frees her is much easier discharge" — a framing move that elides rather than resolves the tension CON identified. PRO's pressure question (Q1) did land a real hit, forcing CON to concede the current system fails the aide administratively, but CON's answer (cheaper/faster proof of the same substantive standard) preserved a coherent distinction between procedural streamlining and lowering the legal bar, and CON used that distinction effectively in Closing. PRO's moral framing, aide example, and gambler analogy were strong and kept this competitive, but the unresolved contradiction about deterrence versus presumption was the load-bearing clash of the debate, and CON controlled it more convincingly through the final two rounds.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2/Closing point that PRO's presumption-based standard, paired with lenders having no visibility into future earnings, cannot simultaneously satisfy PRO's claim that "filing-cost alone" deters gaming — forcing the choice between no standard change (CON's position) or a standard that guts the deterrent PRO relies on. PRO never directly answers the lender-rebuttal-impossibility point.</best_rebuttal>
